    02 / LIBRARY

    The revision material that earns marks.

    Use these as compact recall sheets. Read one module, cover it, reproduce the rules, then solve questions without looking back.

    Arithmetic core

    • Percentage: x% of y = y% of x. Successive changes a%, b% give net a + b + ab/100.
    • Profit & loss: Profit% = profit ÷ cost price × 100. Discount always applies to marked price.
    • Ratio: if A:B = m:n, write A=mk and B=nk before using the total.
    • Average: total = average × count. Replacement changes total by new − old.
    • Mixture: allegation ratio = (dearer − mean):(mean − cheaper).
    Speed rule: memorise fractions 1/2 to 1/20 as percentages; they appear inside almost every arithmetic shortcut.

    Formula strip


    Simple interest

    Two-year compound interest

    Rates add when working together

    Use relative speed for trains

    Fast factorisation

    Triangle area

    Visual anchors — see the formula

    Time & work shortcut

    If A finishes in 12 days and B in 18, take total work as LCM 36 units. Rates are 3 and 2 units/day; together they need 36/5 = 7.2 days.

    Geometry, algebra & data interpretation

    Geometry essentials

    • Triangle angles sum to 180°. Exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles.
    • Pythagoras: . Memorise 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.
    • Circle: circumference ; area ; angle in a semicircle is 90°.
    • Cylinder volume ; cone volume ; sphere volume .

    DI discipline

    • Read units and base year before calculating.
    • Approximate only after checking answer-option gaps.
    • Percentage change = difference ÷ original, not new value.
    • For pie charts, 1% = 3.6° and 25% = 90°.

    Series & analogy

    • For number series, inspect first differences, then second differences, ratios, alternating terms and squares/cubes.
    • For letter series, map A=1…Z=26 and test constant or alternating shifts.
    • In analogy, state the relation in words before checking options: “tool → function”, “part → whole”, “cause → effect”.
    Do not overfit. SSC series usually use the simplest rule that explains every term.

    Logic toolkit

    • Syllogism: draw minimum-valid Venn diagrams; never assume converse.
    • Venn counting: A∪B = A+B−A∩B.
    • Coding: check reversal, alphabet position, pair sums (A+Z=27) and word-length first.
    • Direction: draw north upward and track net horizontal/vertical displacement.
    • Blood relation: assign generation levels (+1 parent, 0 peer, −1 child).

    Fast visual reasoning

    For mirror images, left and right reverse but top and bottom stay. For water images, top and bottom reverse. In paper folding, mentally unfold in exact reverse order; every fold mirrors existing holes. In embedded figures, trace angles and line lengths rather than the whole outline.

    Grammar rules that repeat

    • A singular subject takes a singular verb; phrases between subject and verb do not change agreement.
    • “Each/every/either/neither” takes a singular verb.
    • With “not only…but also” and “either…or”, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
    • Use fewer for countable nouns and less for uncountable quantities.
    • Parallel ideas need parallel forms: “reading, writing and revising”.

    Vocabulary engine

    • bene- good: benefit, benevolent
    • mal- bad: malfunction, malevolent
    • cred- believe: credible, incredulous
    • loqu- speak: eloquent, soliloquy
    • chrono- time: chronology, synchronize
    Learn every word as: meaning + one collocation + one opposite. Isolated word lists decay quickly.

    Comprehension method

    1. Read the question stem first; mark whether it asks fact, inference, tone or vocabulary.
    2. For factual questions, choose only what the passage states.
    3. For inference, reject options that add a new claim or use absolute words such as “always”.
    4. For cloze tests, check grammar, meaning and collocation—in that order.

    Polity & history spine

    • The Constitution was adopted on 26 Nov 1949 and came into force on 26 Jan 1950.
    • Fundamental Rights are in Part III; Directive Principles in Part IV; Fundamental Duties in Part IVA.
    • Money Bills can be introduced only in Lok Sabha; the Speaker certifies them.
    • 1857: major uprising; 1885: INC founded; 1919: Jallianwala Bagh; 1930: Dandi March; 1942: Quit India.

    Science & geography spine

    • SI units: force—newton; power—watt; pressure—pascal; charge—coulomb.
    • Vitamin C deficiency: scurvy; D: rickets; iron deficiency: anaemia.
    • Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states.
    • Western Ghats intercept the southwest monsoon; rain-shadow lies east of the range.
    • Earth rotates west to east, causing sunrise to appear in the east.

    Economy basics

    • Repo rate: rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to banks against securities.
    • Inflation: sustained rise in the general price level; CPI tracks retail inflation.
    • Fiscal deficit: total expenditure minus total non-debt receipts.
    • GDP measures final goods and services produced within a country in a period.

    Computer basics

    • CPU includes control unit and arithmetic logic unit; RAM is volatile memory.
    • 1 byte = 8 bits. An operating system manages hardware and software resources.
    • HTTPS encrypts browser–server traffic; phishing impersonates a trusted source.
    • Spreadsheet formulas begin with =; absolute cell references use $ signs.
    03 / PLAN

    Six weeks. One repeatable rhythm.

    Each week follows the same loop: concept → timed set → error log → spaced revision. Allocate more time to the two weakest subjects after the diagnostic.

    WEEK 01

    Baseline

    One full diagnostic. Arithmetic fundamentals, grammar agreement, basic series and static-GK map.

    WEEK 02

    Core build

    Percentage/ratio, coding/syllogism, parts of speech, polity and modern history.

    WEEK 03

    Expand

    Time-work/speed, visual reasoning, vocabulary roots, geography and science.

    WEEK 04

    Exam mode

    Algebra/geometry, mixed reasoning, comprehension, economy and computer basics.

    WEEK 05

    Pressure

    Three sectional tests and two full mocks. Re-solve every wrong and guessed answer.

    WEEK 06

    Convert

    Five full mocks, formula/vocabulary recall, current-affairs revision and sleep discipline.

    1. Number System & Arithmetic

    SSC's quantitative section is won or lost on speed. Every shortcut below is one the SSC paper repeats in disguised form; learn the pattern, not the individual question.

    1.1 Divisibility rules — the five-minute screen

    A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits are divisible by 4 (1,324: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 ✓). By 8, last three digits divisible by 8. By 11: (sum of digits in odd positions) − (sum of digits in even positions) is 0 or a multiple of 11. Test 918,082: odd-position digits 9,8,8 → 25; even-position digits 1,0,2 → 3; 25 − 3 = 22 = 2 × 11 ✓. By 7: drop the last digit, subtract twice it from the rest; repeat. 2,031 → 203 − 2 = 201 → 20 − 2 = 18, not divisible by 7 ✗. These rules shortcut half of all "find the missing digit" questions.

    1.2 HCF and LCM — the co-prime shortcut

    For fractions, HCF(a/b, c/d) = HCF(a,c) ÷ LCM(b,d) and LCM(a/b, c/d) = LCM(a,c) ÷ HCF(b,d). Exam example: HCF of 2/3, 4/5 and 6/7 = HCF(2,4,6)/LCM(3,5,7) = 2/105. Remainder trap: "Find the greatest number that divides 129, 223 and 317 leaving remainders 3, 5 and 7" — subtract remainders first: 126, 218, 310 → HCF = 2. Students who skip the subtraction step always lose this mark.

    1.3 Fractions as percentages — memorise, don't calculate

    SSC arithmetic lives inside these conversions: 1/2 = 50%, 1/3 ≈ 33⅓%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 ≈ 16⅔%, 1/7 ≈ 14.28%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 ≈ 11.11%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/11 ≈ 9.09%, 1/12 ≈ 8.33%, 1/15 ≈ 6.67%, 1/20 = 5%, 1/25 = 4%. Example: 12.5% of 4,800 = 4,800/8 = 600 in one step. And the reverse symmetry: x% of y = y% of x — so 16% of 25 = 25% of 16 = 4.

    1.4 Successive percentage changes

    Two successive changes a% and b%: (use negative sign for decreases). A price rises 20% then falls 20%: 20 − 20 − (20×20)/100 = −4%. Trap: this is not zero — returning to the original value always needs a bigger percentage rise than the fall was, because the base grew. For three changes, apply the formula twice in sequence.

    1.5 Profit, loss, discount — watch the base

    Profit% and loss% are always on cost price; discount% is always on marked price. Linking them: if MP is 25% above CP and a 20% discount is given, SP = 1.25 × 0.8 × CP = CP — break even. General shortcut: successive mark-up m% and discount d% give net on cost. False-weight trap (a SSC favourite): a dishonest shopkeeper claims to sell at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. = 11.11%. The base is what he actually gives, not 1000.

    1.6 Simple and compound interest

    . For CI, the tree method beats the formula for 2–3 years: at 10%, ₹10,000 → year 1 interest 1,000; year 2 interest 1,000 + 100 (interest on interest). Two-year shortcut: . At r = 20: CI = P × 0.44. Difference trick: CI − SI for 2 years = ; for 3 years = . Example: CI − SI = ₹60 at 10% for 2 years → P × (0.1)² = 60 → P = 6,000. Half-yearly compounding: halve the rate, double the time periods.

    1.7 Ratio, allegation, averages

    Always convert ratios to "k" form: A:B:C = 2:3:4 and total 180 → A = 2k, 2k+3k+4k = 180 → k = 20 → A = 40. Alligation: mix a ₹40/kg and ₹55/kg rice to get ₹46/kg → ratio = (55−46):(46−40) = 9:6 = 3:2 (cheaper:dearer). Average trap: average speed for equal distances at v₁ and v₂ is the harmonic mean 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂), never (v₁+v₂)/2. Averages change on replacement: new average = old average + (new − old)/count.

    1.8 Time & work, time & speed

    LCM method: A does a job in 12 days, B in 18 → total work = LCM = 36 units → rates 3 and 2 units/day → together 36/5 = 7.2 days. Efficiency shortcut: A is twice as efficient as B → A takes half the days. For trains: relative speed adds when moving toward each other, subtracts when same direction — and always convert km/h to m/s with ×5/18. A 240 m train at 72 km/h (20 m/s) crosses a pole in 240/20 = 12 s. Boats: downstream = u+v, upstream = u−v; still-water speed = (down + up)/2.

    Common traps to drill: (1) percentage points vs percent — a rise from 20% to 25% is a 5 point rise but a 25% increase; (2) average of averages without weights; (3) using marked price as the base for profit; (4) forgetting unit conversion in speed questions.

    2. Algebra, Geometry & Mensuration

    This is SSC's highest-weightage quantitative block. Geometry questions are theorem-recall under time pressure; algebra questions are identity-recognition. Drill both as patterns.

    2.1 Algebraic identities — recognise, don't expand

    Core set: ; ; ; ; ; ; ; . Exam example: if x + 1/x = 5, then x² + 1/x² = 5² − 2 = 23, and x³ + 1/x³ = 5³ − 3×5 = 110. The −2 and −3x pattern: for x + 1/x = k, and . Memorise these two; they appear almost every year.

    2.2 Solving systems fast

    If x + y = a and xy = b, then x, y are roots of . Elimination shortcut: in 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x + y = 14, notice doubling the first gives 4x + 6y = 24; subtract the second → 5y = 10 → y = 2, x = 3. Always scan for a combination that eliminates in one step before doing full substitution. Degree trap: x² = 25 gives x = ±5; if the question says "positive root", the answer is 5 only — SSC plants ±5 as an option.

    2.3 Triangle theorems that score

    Angles sum to 180°; exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Centroid divides each median in ratio 2:1 (vertex side longer). Incentre (angle bisectors meet) is the centre of the inscribed circle; circumcentre (perpendicular bisectors meet) is the centre of the circumscribed circle — for a right triangle the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = 2 × circumradius. Similarity: if two triangles are similar with side ratio m:n, their area ratio is m²:n². Pythagoras triples to know cold: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29.

    2.4 Circles — the four theorems

    (1) Angle in a semicircle is 90°. (2) The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through that point. (3) Two tangents drawn from one external point are equal in length. (4) If two chords intersect inside a circle, (segment₁)(segment₂) of one = (segment₁)(segment₂) of the other — the intersecting-chords rule. Exam example: two chords AB and CD intersect at O with AO = 4, OB = 6, CO = 3 → OD = (4×6)/3 = 8. Trap: "angle subtended by the same arc at the centre is double the angle at the circumference" — students invert this under pressure.

    2.5 Quadrilaterals & polygons

    Interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n−2)×180°; each interior angle of a regular polygon = (n−2)×180°/n. Regular hexagon: each angle 120°, and it is exactly six equilateral triangles — area = 6 × (√3/4)s². Rhombus: area = ½ × d₁ × d₂; side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)². Parallelogram area = base × height; diagonals of a rectangle are equal, diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors.

    2.6 Coordinate geometry (Tier-2 weight)

    Distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²]. Midpoint = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2). Slope = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁); parallel lines share slopes, perpendicular lines have slopes m and −1/m. Shortcut: for intercepts, the line x/a + y/b = 1 cuts the axes at (a,0) and (0,b) — read them straight off.

    2.7 Mensuration — formulas plus the combine rule

    Areas: triangle (also Heron: ); trapezium ½(sum of parallel sides)×height; circle . Volumes: cylinder ; cone ; sphere ; hemisphere ; . Combine rule: when a solid is melted and recast, volume is conserved — equate volumes. When a wire is drawn thinner, volume stays constant. Scaling trap: if every linear dimension doubles, area ×4 and volume ×8. A sphere's radius tripled → volume becomes 27×. Frustum of a cone (a SSC favourite): volume = . Surface areas: cylinder total = ; sphere = ; cone curved = where .

    Common traps to drill: (1) diameter vs radius — halve before squaring; (2) curved vs total surface area (a "hollow pipe" question usually wants total including inner surface and rims); (3) mixing units — convert cm and m before multiplying; (4) in "recast" questions, equating surface areas instead of volumes.

    3. Trigonometry & Data Interpretation

    Trigonometry in SSC is a closed set of about twenty facts; Data Interpretation is a closed set of about ten calculations. Both reward a fixed routine.

    3.1 The standard-angle table — learn the pattern, not the table

    For 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, sin values are √(0)/2, √(1)/2, √(2)/2, √(3)/2, √(4)/2 — i.e. 0, ½, 1/√2, √3/2, 1. Cos runs the same list backwards; tan = sin/cos. So tan 60° = √3, cot 30° = √3, sec 60° = 2, cosec 30° = 2. Complementary pairs: sin(90°−θ) = cos θ; tan(90°−θ) = cot θ; sec(90°−θ) = cosec θ. Example: sin 35° × sec 55° = sin 35° × cosec 35° = 1.

    3.2 The three identities

    (1) ; (2) ; (3) . From these, any expression with "1 +" or "1 −" plus a square trig function collapses. Exam example: . And . Watch for the difference-of-squares shape hiding inside trig expressions.

    3.3 Heights and distances

    Angle of elevation = angle of depression for the same two points (alternate interior angles). Standard setup: a tower of height h, shadow angle 45° → distance = h. If the angle is 30°, ; if 60°, . Two-observation method: from points 60 m apart on the same line, angles of elevation to a tower top are 30° and 60° → let distance of nearer point be x: → → → . Draw the diagram every time — the marks come from the setup, not the algebra.

    3.4 Max/min and range

    ranges between and . So 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ maxes at 5. sin²θ + cos²θ is always 1 regardless of θ — an option that says otherwise is always wrong. Trap: sin θ and cos θ can be negative (for θ beyond 90°), but SSC Tier-1 heights questions stay in 0–90°; don't overcomplicate.

    3.5 Data Interpretation — the fixed routine

    Step 1: read the units (₹ crore vs ₹ lakh ruins answers), the base year, and whether the graph is cumulative. Step 2: for each question, write the exact formula before touching numbers — percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100, where "old" is the earlier year, never the larger one. Step 3: approximate only after checking the gaps between options; if options are 12.5%, 14.2%, 16.6%, 18.1%, rounding 1/7 to 14% is safe, but if two options differ by 0.5%, calculate exactly.

    3.6 DI calculation shortcuts

    Percentage change: 240 → 300 is +25% (60/240). Ratio questions: cancel common factors before dividing — 450:600 = 3:4, then compare. Average across years: total ÷ number of years; don't average the percentages unless the bases are equal. Pie charts: 1% = 3.6°; a 25% sector is exactly 90°. Convert degree-to-value with one multiplication: value = (degrees/360) × total. "How many times" vs "percent more": 800 vs 200 is 4 times but 300% more — SSC sets both phrasings as adjacent options.

    Common traps to drill: (1) computing percentage change on the wrong base (using the new value as denominator); (2) mixing absolute and percentage scales on dual-axis graphs; (3) in pie charts, comparing two years' pies without scaling by the different totals; (4) misreading "of" vs "more than" in trig-free DI wordings.

    4. Verbal Reasoning

    Reasoning is the most scoring SSC section because every question type follows a finite rulebook. Learn the checklist per type and apply it mechanically.

    4.1 Number series — the difference ladder

    Write first differences; if they aren't constant, write second differences. 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 → differences 4, 6, 8, 10 → next difference 12 → 42. If second differences are constant, it's quadratic. Other families: prime sequences (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13); squares/cubes ± n (1, 8, 27, 64 → n³; but 2, 9, 28, 65 = n³+1); multiplication chains (3, 6, 18, 72 → ×2, ×3, ×4 → next ×5 = 360); interleaved pairs (split odd/even positions into two series). Digit-operation series: 12 → 12×2+1 = 25, ×2+2 = 52 — check the multiplier against position number.

    4.2 Letter and mixed series

    Number the alphabet: A=1 … Z=26, and remember pairs summing to 27 (A+Z, B+Y, C+X …). In a letter series, convert to positions first: C, F, J, O, ? → 3, 6, 10, 15 → gaps 3, 4, 5 → next gap 6 → 21 = U. Skip-letter pattern: "skip 1, skip 2, skip 3" gives B(1), D(2), G(3), K(4) → next skip 5 → Q. For alphanumeric mixed series (A1, C3, F6, J10 …), decode letters and numbers as two independent series.

    4.3 Coding-decoding — four checks in order

    Check (1) position sums: A+Z = 27 — if P(16) codes to K(11), 16+11 = 27, so it's a reverse-pair code; (2) reversal of the whole word; (3) constant shift (Caesar); (4) position-dependent shift (+1, +2, +3 …). Exam example: "MANGO" → "NZNHL": M(13)→N(+1), A(1)→Z(−1 or +25), N(14)→N(0), G(7)→H(+1), O(15)→L(−3). Shifts: +1, −1, 0, +1, −3 — irregular; check pairs: 13+14=27? N+Z… better test reverse-pairs per letter: M+N? no. Try alternating +1/−1 on first four, then the last breaks it — so look again: this code is actually vowels→previous letter? A→Z ✓ (previous with wrap), O→L ✗. Real SSC codes are always clean; if your pattern needs an exception, restart with the 27-pair test on each letter: 13+14? Check N(14) vs N(14): 14+14=28 no… Here M(13)→N(14) sums to 27 ✓, A(1)→Z(26) sums to 27 ✓, N(14)→N(14) sums to 28 ✗ — so it's not pure reverse-pair; the middle letter is unchanged (palindrome-mirror code), a known SSC variant: reverse pairs for all letters except the middle one.

    4.4 Blood relations — generation levels

    Assign levels: grandparents +2, parents +1, self/peers 0, children −1, grandchildren −2. "A is B's father's sister's son" — father (+1), his sister (+1), her son (0) → cousin. Trap: "only son/daughter" fixes uniqueness — "the only son of my grandfather" when the speaker is male = the speaker's father; when female = her uncle or father depending on siblings. Draw a tiny tree with gender marks rather than reasoning in words.

    4.5 Direction sense

    Draw north up. Track net displacement as (east-west, north-south) components. "5 km north, then 3 km east, then 5 km south" → net (3 east, 0) → 3 km east of start. Shadow rule: at sunrise shadows point west; at sunset they point east — if A's shadow falls to B's left at sunrise, B is facing north. For "shortest distance", use Pythagoras on the net components.

    4.6 Syllogisms — minimum-valid Venn

    Draw the weakest diagram the premises allow: "All A are B" — draw A fully inside B (but B may extend beyond). "Some A are B" — overlap the circles partially. A conclusion is valid only if it holds in every possible diagram. Golden traps: (1) never assume the converse — "All A are B" does NOT imply "All B are A"; (2) two negative premises ("No A is B", "No B is C") yield no conclusion; (3) "Some A are B" + "Some B are C" yields nothing about A and C — the B's may be different B's. The "either/or" case: "Some A are B" with premises allowing both "All A are B" and "No A is B"… only when both are individually possible does the either/or pair follow.

    4.7 Statements: conclusions, assumptions, arguments

    Conclusion must follow necessarily — reject anything needing outside knowledge or containing absolutes ("always", "never", "all") unless the statement itself is absolute. Assumption is the unstated bridge: negate a candidate assumption; if the statement collapses, it was assumed. Strong argument: directly addresses the issue and is fact-based ("banning X reduces Y, as shown by data"); weak arguments appeal to examples, analogies, or consequences ("other countries do it"). Cause-effect: if both events share a stated common cause, neither caused the other — mark "both are effects of a common cause".

    4.8 Ranking, order, seating

    For ranks: position from top + position from bottom − 1 = total. "7th from left, 12th from right" → 18 people. Seating: fix one person to break rotational symmetry, place clockwise, and keep "left/right" relative to facing direction — for a circle facing the centre, each person's left is your clockwise direction. In linear rows facing north, right is your right; facing south it flips. Write "≥" constraints as inequalities and propagate.

    Common traps to drill: (1) in series, forcing a difference pattern when it's a digit-operation or interleaved pair; (2) in coding, accepting a pattern with one exception; (3) in syllogisms, drawing the "nicest" Venn instead of the minimum-valid one; (4) in blood relations, assuming the speaker's gender; (5) in direction, forgetting that turning left/right depends on current facing.

    5. Non-Verbal Reasoning

    Non-verbal questions test rule-following, not imagination. Every figure series runs on a small set of operations; your job is to identify which one is active.

    5.1 Mirror and water images — the axis rule

    Mirror (vertical axis at the side): left and right swap, top and bottom stay. Water (horizontal axis below): top and bottom swap, left and right stay. Speed check: for a mirror image, read the figure left-to-right — the leftmost element becomes the rightmost. Letters with vertical symmetry (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) look identical in a mirror; letters with horizontal symmetry (B, C, D, E, H, I, O, X) look identical in water. Digits 0, 1, 8 are unchanged in both. Trap: SSC sometimes places the mirror on the top — then it behaves like a water image. Always locate the mirror line first.

    5.2 Paper folding and cutting

    Unfold in exact reverse order; each unfold mirrors every existing hole across the last fold line. Method: number the folds 1-2-3, then undo 3-2-1, reflecting the pattern each time. A hole punched once in a twice-folded paper appears 4 times. Counting shortcut: final hole count = (holes punched) × 2^(number of folds) — but only if each fold doubled the layers and the punch went through all layers. Holes near a fold line land close together after unfolding; far from it, they spread symmetrically.

    5.3 Figure series — the operation menu

    Check in this order: (1) rotation — an element or the whole figure turns by a fixed angle each step (45°, 90°, 180°); (2) movement — an element shifts position along a fixed path (clockwise around corners); (3) addition/subtraction — one element added or removed per step; (4) alternation — odd and even positions follow two different rules (split the series); (5) shading/number change — count of shaded parts or lines changes by a fixed amount. Exam habit: pick one distinctive element and track only it through the series before looking at the whole figure — this defeats the "everything changes" confusion.

    5.4 Figure analogy and classification

    Analogy (A : B :: C : ?): extract the transformation from A to B — rotated 90°? inside-out? element count doubled? — then apply it to C. Common transformations: mirror across a diagonal, black↔white swap, outer shape becomes inner, number of sides ±1. Odd one out: find the property four share — all have even sides, all are divided into equal parts, all have the dot inside the triangle — the figure breaking it is the answer. Check rotation first: sometimes the "odd" figure is just rotated, which doesn't count as different.

    5.5 Counting figures

    Count systematically by size: count all smallest triangles, then ones made of 2 small units, then 3, and so on. Formula shortcuts: in a triangle subdivided into n rows of small triangles, total triangles = n(n+2)(2n+1)/8 (n even) — for n = 4: 4×6×9/8 = 27. Squares in an n×n grid: n² + (n−1)² + … + 1². Rectangles in an m×n grid of small rectangles: [m(m+1)/2] × [n(n+1)/2]. Trap: overlapping figures — draw and number each region, or you'll double-count.

    5.6 Dice

    Opposite faces never appear together in one view. Two-view method: find the face common to two positions; the faces adjacent to it in the two views, in order, are opposites pairwise. Standard dice: opposite faces sum to 7 — but SSC also uses non-standard dice, so derive from the views, don't assume. Unfolded-net rule: in a cube net, faces with exactly one face between them in a straight line are opposites; the "T" junction's stem-end and the junction face are opposites.

    5.7 Embedded figures and completion

    For embedded figures, match angles and line lengths, not the overall look — rotate the question figure mentally. For figure completion (which piece fits the gap), check the continuity of lines at the boundary: lines entering the gap must continue into the answer piece. Eliminate options whose edge lines don't align before comparing patterns.

    Common traps to drill: (1) confusing mirror with water image when the axis isn't labelled; (2) in paper cutting, unfolding in the wrong order; (3) missing alternation in series (always test odd/even split); (4) in dice, assuming standard 7-sum opposites; (5) counting figures by eye instead of by size-class.

    6. English Grammar

    SSC English error-spotting recycles a fixed set of about thirty rules. The list below is the high-frequency core — every rule here has appeared in recent papers.

    6.1 Subject–verb agreement

    The verb agrees with the subject, not with nouns trapped between them: "The list of items is long." Each, every, either, neither, one, nobody, somebody → singular verb: "Each of the boys has a pen." With either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "Neither the students nor the teacher was present." Fraction/collective subjects: "Half of the apples are rotten" (countable → plural) but "Half of the milk is gone" (uncountable → singular). Amounts, distances, time as a single unit → singular: "Ten kilometres is a long walk." Trap: "The number of" → singular ("The number of cases is rising") but "A number of" → plural ("A number of cases were reported").

    6.2 Tenses — the four decisions

    (1) Simple past vs present perfect: use present perfect only when the past connects to now — "I have lived here since 2010" vs "I lived there in 2010." (2) Since + point of time, for + duration: "since Monday", "for three days". (3) Past perfect needs two past events: "When I arrived, the train had left." (4) Universal truths and habits → simple present even in past-tense narratives: "He said that the sun rises in the east." Sequence trap: after "hardly/scarcely…when" and "no sooner…than" — "No sooner had he arrived than it rained."

    6.3 Articles

    A/an for first mention, the for known/second mention. No article before: proper nouns, meals ("have dinner"), languages, sports, plural generic nouns ("Dogs are loyal"). Fixed uses of "the": rivers, seas, mountain ranges (the Himalayas — but "Mount Everest", no the), newspapers, superlatives, ordinals, musical instruments ("play the guitar"), inventions ("the telephone"). Trap: "a university" / "a European" — the article follows sound, not spelling (consonant sound → a).

    6.4 Prepositions — learn collocations, not rules

    High-frequency pairs: accused of, afraid of, apply for (a job) but apply to (a person), arrive at (small place) / in (city), belong to, capable of, compared with (things) / to (likening), consist of, depend on, die of (disease) / from (cause), differ from, good at, insist on, interested in, junior/senior/inferior/superior to (never "than"), married to, prefer to (not "than" — "prefer tea to coffee"), proud of, refer to, suffer from, succeed in, wait for. Time: at (clock time), on (days/dates), in (months/years/parts of day).

    6.5 Pronouns and determiners

    Who (subject) vs whom (object): "the officer whom I met" — test by substituting he/him. Reflexives for emphasis or when subject = object: "He did it himself"; never "Myself did it." Fewer vs less: fewer + countable ("fewer books"), less + uncountable ("less water"). Much + uncountable, many + countable. Each other (two) vs one another (more than two). "One" as pronoun repeats with "one's": "One must do one's duty."

    6.6 Conditionals and modals

    Type 1 (real): "If it rains, we will stay." Type 2 (unreal present): "If I were rich, I would travel." Type 3 (unreal past): "If he had studied, he would have passed." Modal traps: "had better" + base verb ("You had better leave"); "would rather" + base verb; "used to" (past habit) vs "be used to" + gerund ("I am used to working late"). After modals (can, must, should, may), always the base verb — "He should go", never "goes".

    6.7 Voice and reported speech

    Active→passive: object becomes subject, verb → be + past participle, tense preserved: "She wrote a letter" → "A letter was written by her." Trap: intransitive verbs have no passive — "He laughed" cannot become passive. Reported speech: backshift tenses (present→past, past→past perfect), shift "this"→"that", "now"→"then", "tomorrow"→"the next day". "He said, 'I am busy'" → "He said that he was busy." Questions become statements: "He asked where I lived" (no question mark, no inversion).

    6.8 Parallel structure and misc. error-spotting

    Parallel ideas need parallel forms: "She likes reading, writing, and revising" (not "to revise"). Comparisons compare like with like: "The climate of Delhi is hotter than that of Shimla" — never "than Shimla". Double negatives cancel wrongly: "I don't know nothing" is an error. "Neither…nor" with two singular subjects → singular verb. Avoid "more better", "most fastest" — double comparatives are always wrong.

    Common traps to drill: (1) "the number of" vs "a number of"; (2) nearer-subject agreement with either/or; (3) junior/senior + "to" not "than"; (4) since/for mix-ups; (5) question-word order surviving into reported speech ("He asked where did I live" ✗).

    7. Vocabulary, Idioms & Comprehension

    SSC English vocabulary is a closed, recycled pool. Roots unlock hundreds of words at once; idioms and one-word substitutions repeat year after year; comprehension rewards method, not speed-reading.

    7.1 Root-based word learning

    Learn each word as meaning + one collocation + one opposite. High-yield roots: bene- good (benevolent, beneficial, benediction); mal- bad (malfunction, malevolent, malicious); cred- believe (credible, incredulous, credentials); loqu-/locu- speak (eloquent, loquacious, soliloquy); chrono- time (chronology, chronic, synchronize); therm- heat (thermal, thermometer); demo- people (democracy, demographic); dict- say (dictate, verdict, contradict); graph- write (biography, autograph); phil- love (philanthropy, philosophy); mis- wrong/hate (misunderstand, misanthrope); pre- before (predict, precede); sub- under (submerge, subordinate); super- above (superior, superimpose); trans- across (transfer, transparent); uni- one (unanimous, uniform); bi- two (bilingual, bilateral); omni- all (omniscient, omnipotent). Example payoff: meeting "malefactor" for the first time — mal- (bad) + fact (do) = wrongdoer, no dictionary needed.

    7.2 Synonyms and antonyms — the elimination game

    First check part of speech — an adjective can't synonymise a verb. Then check connotation (positive/negative/neutral): "frugal" is positive (thrifty), "stingy" is negative — they are not interchangeable. Common SSC pairs: candid–frank (ant: evasive); diligent–industrious (ant: lazy); obscure–vague (ant: clear); reluctant–unwilling (ant: eager); transparent–clear (ant: opaque); ancient–old (ant: modern); benevolent–kind (ant: cruel); ephemeral–short-lived (ant: eternal); meticulous–careful (ant: careless); audacious–bold (ant: timid). When unsure, eliminate the two options whose meanings you know are wrong — a 50/50 guess beats a blank, and SSC has no negative marking to fear in Tier-1… correction: SSC CGL Tier-1 does carry −0.50 negative marking per wrong answer, so eliminate to 50/50 before guessing, and skip pure guesses.

    7.3 Idioms — the repeating set

    These recur across papers: beat around the bush — avoid the point; by and large — on the whole; a hard and fast rule — a strict, unchangeable rule; at sixes and sevens — in confusion/disorder; burn the midnight oil — study/work late; to bite the dust — to fail/be defeated; a blessing in disguise — a hidden benefit; cut corners — do something cheaply/quickly, sacrificing quality; hit the nail on the head — say exactly the right thing; let the cat out of the bag — reveal a secret; once in a blue moon — very rarely; spill the beans — disclose information; the ball is in your court — it's your turn to act; under the weather — slightly ill; add fuel to the fire — worsen a situation; a wild goose chase — a futile pursuit; barking up the wrong tree — pursuing a mistaken line; break the ice — initiate conversation; cost an arm and a leg — very expensive; on cloud nine — extremely happy. Method: learn the story image behind each idiom once; rote lists decay within days.

    7.4 One-word substitutions

    High-frequency set: omniscient — one who knows everything; omnipotent — all-powerful; invincible — cannot be defeated; incorrigible — cannot be corrected; illegible — cannot be read; inaudible — cannot be heard; ambiguous — having more than one meaning; contemporary — living at the same time; optimist — one who looks on the bright side; pessimist — one who looks on the dark side; ascetic — one who practices self-denial; stoic — indifferent to pleasure and pain; altruist — one who lives for others; egoist — one who is self-centred; bibliophile — lover of books; philanthropist — lover of mankind; orator — skilled public speaker; linguist — one who knows many languages; polyglot — speaking many languages; itinerant — travelling from place to place; refugee — one who flees for safety; emigrant/immigrant — one who leaves/enters a country to settle. Notice how the roots from 7.1 decode half of these.

    7.5 Commonly confused words

    Affect (verb: influence) vs effect (noun: result); adapt (adjust) vs adopt (take up); complement (complete) vs compliment (praise); principal (head/chief) vs principle (rule); stationary (not moving) vs stationery (writing materials); eminent (famous) vs imminent (about to happen); elicit (draw out) vs illicit (illegal); persecute (oppress) vs prosecute (bring to trial); childish (negative) vs childlike (positive). SSC loves the affect/effect and principal/principle pairs — decide by part of speech first.

    7.6 Comprehension — question-first method

    Read the question stems first and label each: fact, inference, tone, or vocabulary. Then read the passage once, underlining only lines that answer a stem. Factual questions: choose only what the passage states — paraphrase is fine, new claims are not. Inference: the answer must follow necessarily; reject options with absolutes ("always", "never", "all") unless the passage is absolute, and reject options that introduce a new claim. Tone: collect the passage's adjectives — "alarming", "promising", "grim" — the tone word must match their charge, not your opinion of the topic. Title questions: the title must cover the whole passage, not just the first paragraph. Skip re-reading: one careful pass with marked stems beats two skims.

    7.7 Cloze test discipline

    For each blank, check in order: (1) grammar — what part of speech fits? (2) meaning — which option fits the sentence? (3) collocation — which option naturally pairs with the neighbouring words? Read the sentence with each candidate inserted; the wrong ones usually break at step 1. For paragraph-level cloze, the passage's overall theme constrains every blank — a positive passage won't take a negative word.

    Common traps to drill: (1) synonym options with the wrong connotation (frugal ≠ stingy); (2) idiom options that sound literal — trust the idiomatic meaning; (3) inference options that are true in real life but not stated in the passage; (4) in cloze tests, picking a word that fits the blank but breaks the collocation with the next word.

    8. Ancient & Medieval History

    History is the highest-weightage section of SSC CGL General Awareness. Roughly 40% of history questions come from Ancient, 35% from Medieval, and most are fact-based — names, dates, founder, capital, battle. This chapter compresses everything SSC has actually asked into one pass.

    Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE)

    • Harappa (Punjab, Pakistan — Ravi river): first site discovered (1921, excavated by Daya Ram Sahni). Gave the civilization its name.
    • Mohenjo-daro (Sindh — Indus river): the Great Bath, the Great Granary, "dancing girl" bronze statue. Excavated 1922 by R.D. Banerji.
    • Lothal (Gujarat): dockyard — evidence of sea trade with Mesopotamia. First man-made port in the world.
    • Dholavira (Gujarat, Kutch): only site with all three divisions — citadel, middle town, lower town. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021.
    • Kalibangan (Rajasthan): ploughed field — earliest evidence of agriculture with a plough.
    • Chanhudaro: bead-making factory; Rakhigarhi (Haryana): largest IVC site in India.
    • Animals on seals: the unicorn (most common), bull, elephant. Script undeciphered — so no written history from IVC.

    Trap: SSC asks "which city had the Great Bath?" — Mohenjo-daro, not Harappa. "Dockyard" = Lothal. "Ploughed field" = Kalibangan.

    Vedic Period & Mahajanapadas (c. 1500–600 BCE)

    • Four Vedas: Rigveda (oldest; 10 mandalas, Gayatri Mantra in Mandala III), Samaveda (music/chants), Yajurveda (sacrificial formulas), Atharvaveda (spells, medicine). Rigveda + Sama + Yajur = Trayi.
    • Upanishads = philosophy ("Vedanta" — end of the Vedas). Smritis, Puranas, and the epics (Ramayana by Valmiki, Mahabharata by Vyasa) came later.
    • 16 Mahajanapadas — the four powerful ones: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti. Capital of Magadha: Rajgir, later Pataliputra (founded by Udayin, Haryanka dynasty).

    Buddhism & Jainism (6th century BCE)

    • Gautama Buddha: born 563 BCE at Lumbini (Nepal), attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya under the Bodhi tree, first sermon at Sarnath (Dhammachakkappavattana), died (Mahaparinirvana) 483 BCE at Kushinagar. These four are the great pilgrimage sites.
    • Buddhist councils: 1st at Rajgir (Ajatashatru, presided Mahakassapa), 2nd at Vaishali (100 years later, split into Sthaviravadins & Mahasanghikas), 3rd at Pataliputra (Ashoka, presided Moggaliputta Tissa), 4th at Kundalvana/Kashmir (Kanishka, presided Vasumitra — Mahayana Buddhism formalized here).
    • Mahavira (24th Tirthankara of Jainism): born 540 BCE at Kundagrama (Vaishali), attained Kaivalya at Jrimbhikagrama, died 468 BCE at Pawapuri. First Tirthankara: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha).
    • Jain principles: Triratna — right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya (added by Mahavira). Jain texts: 12 Angas.

    Trap: Buddha's birthplace Lumbini is in Nepal — SSC loves this. First Buddhist council was right after Buddha's death at Rajgir.

    Mauryan Empire (322–185 BCE)

    • Chandragupta Maurya: founded the empire with Chanakya (Kautilya, author of the Arthashastra). Defeated Seleucus Nicator; Megasthenes (author of Indica) was his ambassador.
    • Ashoka (268–232 BCE): grandson of Chandragupta, son of Bindusara. Kalinga War (261 BCE) transformed him; he adopted Buddhism under Upagupta and sent missionaries (Mahinda & Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka).
    • Ashoka's edicts: inscribed on rocks and pillars in Prakrit (Brahmi script). James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837. Lion Capital of Sarnath is our national emblem.
    • Mauryan decline after Ashoka; last ruler Brihadratha killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga (founded Shunga dynasty).

    Guptas & Post-Guptas (c. 320–550 CE) — the "Golden Age"

    • Chandragupta I: founder of Gupta era (320 CE — Gupta Era starts). Samudragupta: "Napoleon of India" (V.A. Smith), Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayag Prashasti) by Harisena. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya): Ujjain capital, Navaratnas including Kalidasa (Shakuntala, Meghaduta) and Aryabhata.
    • Aryabhata: Aryabhatiya — explained zero's place-value use, Earth's rotation. Nalanda University founded by Kumaragupta I.
    • Huna invasions ended Gupta power. Harshavardhana (606–647 CE): capital Kannauj, wrote Ratnavali, Nagananda, Priyadarshika; his court poet Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita; Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) visited during his reign.

    South India — Cholas (9th–13th century)

    • Rajaraja Chola I: built the Brihadeeswara Temple, Thanjavur (UNESCO site); powerful navy — conquered Sri Lanka and Maldives.
    • Rajendra Chola I: "Gangaikonda Chola" — naval expedition to Southeast Asia (Srivijaya). Local self-government via village assemblies (Uttaramerur inscription) — a favorite SSC question.

    Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)

    • Slave (Mamluk) dynasty: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (founded Sultanate; built Qutb Minar, started by him, completed by Iltutmish; patronized Lakh Baksh), Iltutmish (real founder — introduced silver tanka and copper jital coins), Razia Sultan (only woman ruler of the Sultanate), Balban ("blood and iron").
    • Khilji dynasty: Alauddin Khilji — market control reforms, repelled Mongols, Malik Kafur's southern campaigns; built Alai Darwaza. Amir Khusrau ("Tut-i-Hind," the Parrot of India) was his court poet.
    • Tughlaq dynasty: Muhammad bin Tughlaq — transfer of capital to Daulatabad, token currency (failed experiments), Ibn Battuta (Moroccan traveller, wrote Rehla) visited India in his reign. Firoz Shah Tughlaq — built canals, founded Jaunpur, imposed jaziya on Brahmins.
    • Sayyid then Lodi: Bahlul Lodi, Sikandar Lodi (founded Agra), Ibrahim Lodi — defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

    Mughal Empire (1526–1857)

    • Babur: Panipat 1526 (guns + field artillery won it), Khanwa 1527 (vs Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (vs Medini Rai), Ghaghra 1529. Wrote Baburnama (Tuzk-i-Baburi) in Turkish.
    • Humayun: defeated by Sher Shah Suri at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj/Bilgram (1540); regained throne 1555. Sher Shah introduced the rupiya coin, Grand Trunk Road, land revenue system (zabt).
    • Akbar (1556–1605): regent Bairam Khan; Second Battle of Panipat (1556) vs Hemu; Battle of Haldighati (1576) vs Maharana Pratap; abolished jaziya (1564) and pilgrimage tax (1563); Din-i-Ilahi (1582); built Fatehpur Sikri; court gems — Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal (revenue), Abul Fazl (Ain-i-Akbari, Akbarnama).
    • Jahangir: "chain of justice"; married Nur Jahan; Captain Hawkins & Sir Thomas Roe (British) visited. Shah Jahan (1628–1658): Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne; the "golden age" of architecture.
    • Aurangzeb (1658–1707): longest reign (49 years); reimposed jaziya (1679); executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675); annexed Bijapur & Golconda; died at Ahmednagar. Mughal decline began under his successors.
    • Shivaji (1630–1680): coronation 1674 at Raigad; Ashtapradhan council; guerrilla warfare; killed Afzal Khan (1659). Maratha Empire peaked under the Peshwas — Baji Rao I; Third Battle of Panipat (1761) vs Ahmad Shah Abdali broke Maratha power.

    Quick-recall trick: the four decisive battles of Panipat-family questions — 1526 (Babur beats Ibrahim Lodi), 1556 (Akbar beats Hemu), 1761 (Abdali beats Marathas). For South invasions: Malik Kafur (Khilji's general), not Alauddin himself.

    9. Modern History

    Modern history is SSC's most predictable section: the same battles, acts, sessions, and slogans repeat. Learn the sequence like a timeline — every event causes the next.

    The Europeans arrive (1498–1757)

    • 1498: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut (Kerala) — Portuguese first. 1510: Portuguese capture Goa (Albuquerque). 1600: English East India Company chartered; first factory at Surat (1613). 1664: French East India Company; French settlement at Pondicherry (1674).
    • Battle of Plassey (1757): Robert Clive defeats Siraj-ud-daulah (Nawab of Bengal) — with Mir Jafar's betrayal. Marks the beginning of British rule in India.
    • Battle of Buxar (1764): British defeat the combined forces of Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-daulah (Awadh), and Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor). The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gives the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Odisha.
    • Anglo-Mysore Wars: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan — Tipu dies at Seringapatam (1799), 4th Anglo-Mysore War. Anglo-Maratha Wars end with Maratha defeat (1818); Punjab annexed after the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1849).
    • Governor-Generals to know: Warren Hastings (first GG of Bengal, 1773 Regulating Act); Cornwallis (Permanent Settlement, 1793); Wellesley (Subsidiary Alliance, 1798 — Hyderabad first); Dalhousie (Doctrine of Lapse — Satara first, 1848; annexed Awadh 1856 on "misgovernment"); Canning (last GG of the Company, first Viceroy, 1858).

    Trap: Plassey (1757) vs Buxar (1764) — SSC swaps them. Plassey = Clive vs Siraj; Buxar = triple alliance, Diwani rights. Subsidiary Alliance = Wellesley; Doctrine of Lapse = Dalhousie.

    The Revolt of 1857

    • Immediate trigger: greased cartridges. Mangal Pandey (34th Bengal Native Infantry, Barrackpore) revolts on 29 March 1857; hanged 8 April. Meerut outbreak: 10 May 1857 — sepoys march to Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor.
    • Centers & leaders: Delhi — Bahadur Shah Zafar; Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal; Kanpur — Nana Saheb (Tatya Tope his general); Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai (died June 1858 at Gwalior); Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan; Bihar — Kunwar Singh (aged 80, Jagdishpur).
    • British generals: Delhi — John Nicholson; Lucknow — Havelock & Colin Campbell; Jhansi — Hugh Rose.
    • Result: Company rule ends; Government of India Act 1858 — Crown takes over; Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858, Allahabad, read by Canning). Zafar exiled to Rangoon.

    Birth of the Congress & the national movement

    • Indian National Congress founded December 1885 in Bombay by A.O. Hume (a retired British officer); first president W.C. Bonnerjee; 72 delegates.
    • 1905: Partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon → Swadeshi Movement (boycott of foreign goods). 1906: Muslim League founded at Dhaka (Aga Khan, Mohsin-ul-Mulk). 1907: Surat Split — Moderates vs Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal — the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio).
    • 1911: Bengal partition annulled; capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi (Delhi Durbar, George V).
    • 1916: Lucknow Pact (Congress + League); Home Rule Movement — Annie Besant and Tilak.
    • 1919: Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April), Amritsar — General Dyer; Rowlatt Act ("black act"); Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (dyarchy in provinces).

    The Gandhian era

    • Gandhi returns from South Africa 1915. First Indian satyagrahas: Champaran (1917) — indigo farmers, Bihar; Kheda (1918) — Gujarat peasants; Ahmedabad (1918) — mill workers.
    • Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): launched August 1920 over Jallianwala + Khilafat; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (5 Feb 1922) — Gandhi called it off when a mob killed 22 policemen.
    • 1928: Simon Commission boycott ("Simon, go back"); Lala Lajpat Rai dies from lathi injuries. 1929: Lahore session — Jawaharlal Nehru president, Purna Swaraj declared; first Independence Day observed 26 January 1930.
    • Civil Disobedience (1930): Dandi March — 12 March to 6 April 1930 (Sabarmati to Dandi, 240 miles, 78 followers) to break the salt law. Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931); Second Round Table Conference (Gandhi attends as Congress's sole representative); Poona Pact (1932) — Gandhi vs Ambedkar on separate electorates for depressed classes.
    • Government of India Act 1935: provincial autonomy, federal structure (never implemented), bicameral legislatures; 1937 provincial elections — Congress wins 7 of 11 provinces.
    • Quit India Movement (1942): launched 8 August 1942 (Bombay session); Gandhi's slogan "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro); leaders jailed the same night; underground leadership by Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia.

    Revolutionaries & the road to independence

    • Kakori train robbery (1925): Hindustan Republican Association — Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Chandrashekhar Azad (hanged 1927). Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev hanged 23 March 1931 (Lahore conspiracy — Saunders murder; Central Assembly bomb 1929).
    • Subhas Chandra Bose: founded Forward Bloc (1939); escaped to Germany then Japan; took over the Indian National Army (INA) in 1943 (first raised by Mohan Singh, 1942); slogan "Give me blood, I will give you freedom" ("Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga"); "Jai Hind"; "Dilli Chalo".
    • 1946: Royal Indian Navy mutiny (Bombay); Cabinet Mission; Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946). 1947: Mountbatten Plan (3 June); Indian Independence Act (July 1947); Independence 15 August 1947; Radcliffe drew the boundary lines.
    • Firsts after independence: first Governor-General of independent India — Lord Mountbatten; first Indian Governor-General — C. Rajagopalachari; first President — Rajendra Prasad; first PM — Jawaharlal Nehru; first woman Governor — Sarojini Naidu (UP).

    Memory peg: Dandi March dates (12 Mar – 6 Apr 1930) and Mangal Pandey (29 Mar 1857) are among the most-asked exact dates in SSC. Slogan → leader matching (Do or Die = Gandhi, Jai Hind = Bose, Inquilab Zindabad = Bhagat Singh, Swaraj is my birthright = Tilak, Vande Mataram = Bankim Chandra Chatterjee) appears almost every year.

    10. Geography

    Geography questions are map questions in disguise — rivers, states, passes, and borders. Keep a mental map of India open while reading this chapter.

    India's location & extent

    • Latitude: 8°4′ N to 37°6′ N; Longitude: 68°7′ E to 97°25′ E. Southernmost point: Indira Point (Great Nicobar, 6°4′ N) — earlier called Pygmalion Point.
    • Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) passes through 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram. Trick: G R M C J W T M (west to east).
    • IST = 82.5° E, passing through Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh); India is GMT +5:30. Longest international border: Bangladesh (4,096 km); shortest: Afghanistan (106 km, Wakhan corridor).
    • Land borders (clockwise from west): Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Bangladesh. Maritime neighbours: Sri Lanka, Maldives, Indonesia. McMahon Line = India–China; Radcliffe Line = India–Pakistan; Durand Line = Pakistan–Afghanistan.

    Physical divisions

    • The Himalayas (west to east): Punjab Himalayas → Kumaon → Nepal → Sikkim → Bhutan → Arunachal (Assam Himalayas). Highest Indian peak: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) — world's 3rd highest; Everest (8,849 m) is in Nepal.
    • Northern Plains: formed by Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra alluvium; divisions — Bhabar (porous, at foothills), Terai (marshy), Bhangar (old alluvium), Khadar (new, fertile, floodplains).
    • Peninsular Plateau: oldest landmass; Deccan Trap (basalt, black soil); Western Ghats (Sahyadri — higher, continuous) vs Eastern Ghats (discontinuous). Anai Mudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak south of the Himalayas; Dodabetta highest in the Nilgiris.
    • Coastal plains: Eastern (wider, deltas — Coromandel, Northern Circars) vs Western (narrow — Konkan, Kanara, Malabar). Islands: Andaman & Nicobar (Bay of Bengal; Barren Island — India's only active volcano) and Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea; coral atolls; smallest UT).
    • Mountain passes: Khyber & Bolan (Pakistan); Nathu La & Jelep La (Sikkim–China); Shipki La (Himachal); Bomdi La (Arunachal); Palghat Gap, Bhor Ghat, Thal Ghat (Western Ghats).

    River systems — the exam's favorite map

    • Ganga (2,525 km): originates Gangotri glacier (Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand) as Bhagirathi; meets Alaknanda at Devprayag → called Ganga; enters plains at Haridwar; longest river flowing within India. Left-bank tributaries: Yamuna? No — right bank: Yamuna (joins at Allahabad/Prayagraj), Son. Left bank: Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi ("sorrow of Bihar").
    • Brahmaputra: originates Chemayungdung glacier (Tibet) as Yarlung Tsangpo; enters India at Arunachal (Dihang/Siang), called Brahmaputra in Assam; longest tributary — Majuli is the world's largest river island on it.
    • Indus: originates Bokhar Chu glacier (Tibet); enters India at Ladakh; flows mostly through Pakistan. Tributaries remembered by "Jhe Chen Vi Ra Be Sut" — Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (the Panchnad).
    • Peninsular rivers (mostly east-flowing, forming deltas): Godavari (1,465 km — "Dakshin Ganga," longest peninsular river), Krishna, Kaveri (disputed between Karnataka & Tamil Nadu), Mahanadi (Hirakud dam).
    • West-flowing rivers (form estuaries, no deltas): Narmada (longest west-flowing; originates Amarkantak; flows through a rift valley between Vindhya & Satpura), Tapti/Tapi. Dams on Narmada: Sardar Sarovar.
    • Other key dams: Bhakra-Nangal (Sutlej — highest gravity dam in India, Govind Sagar), Tehri (Bhagirathi — tallest dam in India), Nagarjuna Sagar (Krishna), Hirakud (Mahanadi — longest dam).

    Climate, soils & vegetation

    • Monsoon: caused by differential heating of land and sea. Southwest monsoon hits Kerala ~1 June (branches: Arabian Sea & Bay of Bengal); retreating monsoon (Oct–Nov) gives Tamil Nadu its main rain — Coromandel coast gets maximum rain in winter.
    • Wettest place: Mawsynram (Meghalaya) — edged out Cherrapunji; driest: Jaisalmer/Thar.
    • Soils: Alluvial (plains, most fertile, rice/wheat), Black/Regur (Deccan trap basalt — best for cotton), Red (Tamil Nadu/Karnataka — iron oxide), Laterite (heavy rainfall areas — leached), Desert (Rajasthan), Mountain (Himalayas — tea).
    • Forests: as per ISFR reports, total forest + tree cover ≈ 25% of India's area. Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover; Mizoram the highest percentage. Largest mangrove: Sundarbans (Royal Bengal Tiger). Project Tiger launched 1973 (Jim Corbett was the first reserve).

    Minerals, agriculture & states

    • Coal: Gondwana fields — Jharia (Jharkhand) largest; India is the 2nd largest coal producer (approximate). Iron ore: Odisha, Chhattisgarh (Bailadila), Karnataka (Bababudan hills). Bauxite: Odisha (largest reserves). Mica: Jharkhand/Bihar (Koderma — India leads world production). Petroleum: Digboi (Assam — oldest refinery), Bombay High (offshore, largest).
    • Crops: Rice — West Bengal (largest producer); Wheat — Uttar Pradesh; Cotton — Gujarat/Maharashtra; Sugarcane — Uttar Pradesh; Tea — Assam; Coffee — Karnataka; Jute — West Bengal ("golden fibre"); Rubber — Kerala; Spices — Kerala ("spice garden of India").
    • Rabi (sown Oct–Nov, harvested spring): wheat, barley, mustard, gram. Kharif (sown June–July): rice, maize, cotton, jute, groundnut. Zaid (summer): watermelon, cucumber.
    • State superlatives: largest state by area — Rajasthan; smallest — Goa; most populous — Uttar Pradesh (2011 Census); least populous — Sikkim; highest literacy — Kerala (94%); lowest — Bihar (~61.8%). Longest coastline: Gujarat (~1,600 km).

    Traps: Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through Odisha or Maharashtra. Kosi joins the Ganga from the left, not right. Mawsynram (not Cherrapunji) is the current wettest. Narmada flows west — the classic "which river flows opposite" question.

    11. Polity

    Polity rewards article numbers. SSC asks "which article?" constantly — the numbers below are the ones that repeat. Learn the number with the concept, not alone.

    Making of the Constitution

    • Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed the Constituent Assembly. First meeting: 9 December 1946 (interim chairman Sachchidananda Sinha). Permanent chairman: Dr. Rajendra Prasad. Chairman of the Drafting Committee: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
    • Adopted: 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day). Enforced: 26 January 1950 — chosen because Purna Swaraj was declared on 26 Jan 1930.
    • Took 2 years, 11 months, 18 days; 11 sessions. Originally 395 articles, 8 schedules, 22 parts — now 448+ articles, 12 schedules (approximate, as amended). Longest written constitution in the world.
    • Biggest borrowing: Government of India Act, 1935 (federal structure, governor's office, emergency). Others: Fundamental Rights (USA), DPSP (Ireland), parliamentary system (UK), concurrent list (Australia), amendment procedure (South Africa).

    Preamble & citizenship

    • "We the people of India… Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic." Socialist, Secular, Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (the "mini-Constitution").
    • The Preamble is part of the Constitution — Berubari case (1960) said it wasn't; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled that. It is not justiciable but is the key to interpretation.
    • Citizenship: Part II, Articles 5–11. Single citizenship for the whole country. CAA 2019 amended the Citizenship Act, 1955.

    Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12–35)

    • Art 14: equality before law; Art 15: no discrimination (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth); Art 16: equality in public employment.
    • Art 19: six freedoms — speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession (the 7th, property, was removed by the 44th Amendment).
    • Art 21: protection of life and personal liberty — the most-litigated article; expanded to include privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), dignity, livelihood.
    • Art 23–24: against exploitation — trafficking/forced labour banned; child labour (below 14) banned in hazardous work.
    • Art 25–28: freedom of religion. Art 29–30: cultural & educational rights of minorities.
    • Art 32: right to constitutional remedies — Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. Writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
    • Art 226: High Courts can also issue writs — wider than Art 32 (any legal right, not only fundamental rights).

    DPSP & Fundamental Duties

    • DPSP (Part IV, Art 36–51): borrowed from Ireland; non-justiciable but "fundamental in governance." Key ones: Art 40 (village panchayats), Art 44 (uniform civil code), Art 45 (early childhood care — amended by 86th), Art 48A (environment — 42nd Amendment), Art 50 (separation of judiciary from executive).
    • Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art 51A): added by 42nd Amendment (1976) on Swaran Singh Committee recommendation; originally 10, now 11 (86th Amendment, 2002 added education duty for ages 6–14).

    Union: President, PM, Parliament

    • President (Art 52–62): elected by an electoral college (MPs + MLAs); 5-year term; minimum age 35; oath by the CJI. Impeachment (Art 61) for violation of the Constitution. First President: Rajendra Prasad; first woman: Pratibha Patil.
    • Emergencies: Art 352 (national — war/external aggression/armed rebellion; declared 3 times: 1962, 1971, 1975–77); Art 356 (President's Rule in a state); Art 360 (financial emergency — never used).
    • Vice-President (Art 63–71): ex-officio chairman of the Rajya Sabha; minimum age 35.
    • Prime Minister (Art 75): appointed by the President; must command Lok Sabha majority; first PM: Jawaharlal Nehru (longest-serving); first woman: Indira Gandhi.
    • Parliament (Art 79–88): President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha. Lok Sabha: 543 elected members, 5-year term (can be dissolved). Rajya Sabha: 245 members (233 elected + 12 nominated), permanent body, 1/3 retire every 2 years, 6-year terms.
    • Money Bill (Art 110): can originate only in the Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only delay it 14 days; Speaker certifies. Joint sitting (Art 118) — presided over by the Speaker.
    • Budget: presented on 1 February (since 2017; rail budget merged); Art 112. Vote on account, guillotine, cut motions are budget vocabulary SSC asks.

    Judiciary, states & local government

    • Supreme Court (Art 124–147): established 26 January 1950; first CJI: H.J. Kania; first woman judge: Fathima Beevi; retirement age 65 (SC), 62 (HC). Judicial review is part of the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973 — Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure).
    • High Courts (Art 214–231): oldest — Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1862). First woman HC chief justice: Leila Seth (Himachal Pradesh).
    • Panchayati Raj: 73rd Amendment (1992) — 3 tiers (village/block/district), 1/3 reservation for women (now 50% in many states), 5-year terms. Based on Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957); first implemented in Nagaur, Rajasthan (2 Oct 1959). Urban: 74th Amendment.
    • Election Commission (Art 324): conducts elections; first CEC: Sukumar Sen; voting age lowered 21→18 by the 61st Amendment (1988).
    • Other bodies SSC asks: CAG (Art 148) — "guardian of the public purse"; UPSC (Art 315–323); Finance Commission (Art 280); Attorney General (Art 76) — first: M.C. Setalvad.

    Landmark amendments (memorize the pairs)

    • 42nd (1976): mini-Constitution — Preamble words, DPSP expanded, Fundamental Duties added. 44th (1978): undid Emergency excesses; right to property demoted to legal right (Art 300A).
    • 52nd (1985): anti-defection (Tenth Schedule). 61st (1988): voting age 18. 73rd/74th (1992): panchayats/municipalities.
    • 86th (2002): RTE — Art 21A, free education ages 6–14. 101st (2016): GST. 103rd (2019): 10% EWS reservation.

    Traps: President's oath is administered by the CJI, not the PM. Money bills start in the Lok Sabha only. The Vice-President is NOT a member of the Rajya Sabha but chairs it. "Violation of the Constitution" is the sole impeachment ground — and no President has ever been impeached.

    12. Economy

    Economy questions in SSC are definition-heavy (GDP, inflation, repo rate) plus institution facts (RBI, SEBI, NITI Aayog) and scheme one-liners. Terms first, then the Indian story.

    Core concepts

    • GDP: total value of final goods & services produced within a country's borders in a year. GNP = GDP + net income from abroad. Nominal GDP at current prices; Real GDP at constant (base-year) prices — real growth strips out inflation.
    • Sectors: Primary (agriculture, mining, fishing), Secondary (manufacturing, construction), Tertiary (services). India's GDP mix is roughly: services ~55%, industry ~25–30%, agriculture ~15–20% (approximate, shifting yearly) — yet agriculture employs the largest share of workers (~40%+).
    • Inflation: sustained rise in prices. Measured by CPI (retail, consumer prices — RBI's target metric, 4% ± 2%) and WPI (wholesale). Deflation = falling prices; stagflation = stagnation + inflation together.
    • Fiscal deficit: government spending minus revenue (excluding borrowings) — the borrowing need. Revenue deficit excludes capital items. FRBM Act (2003) targets fiscal discipline.
    • Per capita income = national income ÷ population. National income in India is estimated by the NSO (National Statistical Office); base year currently 2011–12.

    Planning: from Five-Year Plans to NITI Aayog

    • First Five-Year Plan (1951–56): Harrod-Domar model, agriculture focus. Second (1956–61): P.C. Mahalanobis model — heavy industry. Third (1961–66): "self-reliance"; plan holidays followed (1966–69) after wars and drought.
    • Fifth Plan (1974–78): "Garibi Hatao" slogan of Indira Gandhi; Twenty-Point Programme. Rolling Plans under the Janata government. Twelfth Plan (2012–17) was the last — theme "Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth."
    • NITI Aayog (1 January 2015) replaced the Planning Commission. Chairperson: the Prime Minister; CEO appointed separately. It is advisory — cooperative federalism is its motto.
    • 1991 reforms: PM P.V. Narasimha Rao, Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh. LPG — Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization. The New Industrial Policy abolished licensing for most industries.

    Money, banking & RBI

    • RBI established 1 April 1935 (RBI Act, 1934; Hilton Young Commission recommendation); nationalized 1 January 1949; HQ moved from Calcutta to Mumbai (1937). It is India's central bank — issues currency (except the ₹1 coin/note, issued by the Government), banker's bank, forex manager.
    • Monetary policy tools: Repo rate — rate at which RBI lends to banks (raising it tightens money, fights inflation); Reverse repo — RBI borrows from banks; CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio — cash parked with RBI, earns nothing); SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio — liquid assets banks must hold); Bank Rate; Open Market Operations.
    • Currency facts: the ₹ symbol designed by Udaya Kumar Dharmalingam (2010). Coins are minted at Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida. Currency notes bear the RBI Governor's signature; coins bear no signature. Demonetization: 8 November 2016 — ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes withdrawn.
    • Bank nationalization: 14 banks on 19 July 1969 (Indira Gandhi era); 6 more in 1980. SBI: originated as Bank of Bengal (1806) → Imperial Bank (1921) → SBI (1955). NABARD (1982) — agriculture & rural development; SIDBI (1990) — small industries; EXIM Bank (1982).
    • SEBI (1988, statutory 1992) regulates securities markets. IRDAI regulates insurance. PFRDA regulates pensions.
    • Digital: UPI launched 2016 by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India); RuPay is NPCI's card network.

    Budget, taxes & trade

    • Union Budget presented on 1 February (moved from last working day of February in 2017); Rail Budget merged with the Union Budget in 2017 (Bibek Debroy committee). First Indian budget: James Wilson, 1860. First budget of independent India: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty, 1947.
    • GST launched 1 July 2017 — 101st Amendment; "one nation, one tax"; subsumed excise, service tax, VAT. GST Council chaired by the Union Finance Minister (Art 279A). GST is a destination-based tax; alcohol and petroleum are outside GST.
    • Direct taxes: income tax, corporation tax, capital gains. Indirect: GST, customs. Laffer Curve relates tax rates to revenue (occasionally asked).
    • Trade: India runs a trade deficit in merchandise but a surplus in services. Largest trading partner: the USA (approximate, recent years); earlier China. FDI vs FII/FPI: FDI is long-term ownership stake; FII is portfolio/hot money. SEZ — Special Economic Zone (first: Kandla, 1965).

    Schemes SSC keeps asking (launch year + purpose)

    • MGNREGA (2006): 100 days guaranteed rural wage employment. PMJDY (2014): Jan Dhan — universal bank accounts. PM-KISAN (2019): ₹6,000/year to farmer families in 3 instalments.
    • Ayushman Bharat (2018): ₹5 lakh/year health cover per family (PM-JAY). Swachh Bharat (2014): sanitation; Ujjwala (2016): LPG connections.
    • Stand-Up India (2016): bank loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. Start-Up India (2016). Digital India (2015). Make in India (2014).
    • Atal Pension Yojana (2015): pension for unorganized workers. PMSBY/PMJJBY (2015): accident and life insurance for ₹12/₹436 per year.
    • PM Vishwakarma (2023): support for traditional artisans. Lakhpati Didi: SHG women earning ₹1 lakh+/year.

    Traps: RBI issues all currency except the ₹1 note/coin — that's the Government of India's. Repo rate is asked with its direction: hike = anti-inflation. The 12th Plan was the last Five-Year Plan — NITI Aayog is NOT a plan body. "Garibi Hatao" belongs to the 5th Plan era.

    13. General Science

    SSC science is Class 9–10 level: units, laws, common compounds, vitamins, and the human body. This chapter is the full one-line bank, organized so you can revise it in 20 minutes.

    Physics — laws & units

    • Newton's laws: 1st — inertia (a body resists change in motion); 2nd — F = ma; 3rd — every action has an equal and opposite reaction (rocket propulsion).
    • Speed of light: 3 × 10⁸ m/s (vacuum); speed of sound: ~343 m/s in air (faster in water, fastest in solids). Light travels as both wave and particle; sound needs a medium — it cannot travel in vacuum.
    • Ohm's law: V = IR. Electric power: P = VI (watt). Household supply in India: 220 V, 50 Hz. Fuse wire: low melting point alloy (lead + tin).
    • Electromagnetic spectrum (short→long wavelength): gamma → X-ray → UV → visible → infrared → microwave → radio. VIBGYOR is the visible band. Rainbow: refraction + dispersion + internal reflection in droplets. Blue sky: Rayleigh scattering (short wavelengths scatter most).
    • Mirrors & lenses: concave mirror converges (dentist, headlight reflector, shaving); convex mirror diverges (rear-view — "objects closer than they appear"). Convex lens converges (magnifier, camera); concave lens diverges (spectacles for myopia).
    • Pressure & fluids: atmospheric pressure measured by barometer; Pascal's law (hydraulic lift); Archimedes' principle (buoyancy — ships float); Bernoulli's principle (aeroplane lift, atomizer).
    • Heat: SI unit joule; specific heat of water highest among common substances (4.18 J/g°C); black bodies are best absorbers and radiators. Ultrasound (>20 kHz): SONAR, medical imaging; bats navigate with it.
    • Nuclear: fission (splitting — atom bombs, reactors; discovered by Hahn & Strassmann) vs fusion (joining — sun, hydrogen bomb). India's first nuclear test: Smiling Buddha, Pokhran, 18 May 1974; Pokhran-II, 11–13 May 1998.
    • Units: force — newton; work/energy — joule; power — watt; current — ampere; resistance — ohm; frequency — hertz; pressure — pascal; charge — coulomb; loudness — decibel; earthquake — Richter scale; humidity — hygrometer; altitude — altimeter.

    Chemistry — the compound bank

    • Common names (SSC's favorite list): washing soda — Na₂CO₃; baking soda — NaHCO₃; caustic soda — NaOH; quicklime — CaO; slaked lime — Ca(OH)₂; limestone/chalk/marble — CaCO₃; plaster of Paris — CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum — CaSO₄·2H₂O; blue vitriol — CuSO₄·5H₂O; green vitriol — FeSO₄; Epsom salt — MgSO₄; laughing gas — N₂O; dry ice — solid CO₂; heavy water — D₂O.
    • Acids & bases: pH < 7 acidic, > 7 basic, 7 neutral. Strongest acid: fluoroantimonic (commonly asked as sulphuric in school lists — note the context); battery acid = sulphuric acid; stomach acid = HCl; vinegar = acetic acid; citrus = citric acid; ant sting = formic acid. Soap: sodium salts of fatty acids — cleans via micelles.
    • Alloys: brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon; stainless steel = iron + chromium + nickel; solder = lead + tin; German silver = copper + zinc + nickel (contains no silver); amalgam = mercury + another metal.
    • Gases: lightest — hydrogen; most abundant in air — nitrogen (78%), oxygen 21%; noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) — inert; argon fills bulbs; helium in balloons (non-flammable); ozone (O₃) layer absorbs UV.
    • Periodic table: 118 elements; Mendeleev gave the first periodic table; modern law by Moseley (atomic number). Most electronegative: fluorine; most abundant element in Earth's crust: oxygen, then silicon; in the universe: hydrogen.
    • Atomic structure: proton discovered — Rutherford; electron — J.J. Thomson; neutron — Chadwick; nucleus — Rutherford. Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons (C-12, C-14).

    Biology — body & life

    • Cell: discovered by Robert Hooke (1665, cork); cell theory — Schleiden & Schwann. Powerhouse: mitochondria; kitchen: chloroplast (photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂); suicide bags: lysosomes; control center: nucleus. DNA double helix: Watson & Crick (1953, with Franklin's data).
    • Blood: ABO groups discovered by Karl Landsteiner. Universal donor: O−; universal recipient: AB+. RBCs live ~120 days, made in bone marrow; haemoglobin carries oxygen (iron). Normal BP: 120/80 mmHg. Blood clotting: platelets + fibrin; vitamin K needed.
    • Human body numbers: 206 bones (babies ~300); longest: femur; smallest: stapes (ear); largest organ: skin; largest internal organ: liver; largest cell: ovum; smallest cell: sperm (often asked as "mycoplasma" for smallest living cell); longest cell: neuron. Normal body temp: 37°C / 98.6°F. 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total).
    • Vitamins & deficiency: A — night blindness (retinol); B1 — beriberi; B3 — pellagra; B12 — anaemia; C — scurvy (ascorbic acid; richest source: amla); D — rickets (sunshine vitamin, calcium absorption); E — fertility/antioxidant; K — blood clotting. Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B-complex, C.
    • Hormones: insulin (pancreas — diabetes when deficient); thyroxine (thyroid — iodine needed, goitre when deficient); adrenaline (adrenal — "fight or flight"); growth hormone (pituitary); testosterone/estrogen (sex hormones).
    • Diseases: malaria — Plasmodium parasite via Anopheles mosquito; dengue/chikungunya — virus via Aedes; TB — Mycobacterium tuberculosis (bacteria); cholera/typhoid — bacteria (water-borne); AIDS — HIV (virus); rabies — virus; polio — virus (vaccine: Salk/Sabin). BCG vaccine: tuberculosis. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin (1928).
    • Plants: photosynthesis in chlorophyll; transpiration through stomata; xylem carries water up, phloem carries food. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Rhizobium (legume roots). Largest flower: Rafflesia; tallest tree: redwood/sequoia; national tree: banyan.

    Traps: universal donor is O− (not O+), recipient AB+ (not AB−). Sound cannot travel in a vacuum — light can. The pH of human blood is ~7.4 (slightly alkaline). Washing soda vs baking soda vs caustic soda — SSC rotates these every year; the formulas above are the whole game.

    14. Static GK + Current Affairs 2025–26

    Static GK is pure memory — the same one-liners appear year after year. Current affairs below are verified against web sources as of September 2026; exact figures are approximate, so cross-check totals before trusting them blindly.

    Firsts in India (the eternal list)

    • First President: Rajendra Prasad; first PM: Jawaharlal Nehru; first woman PM: Indira Gandhi; first woman President: Pratibha Patil; first woman Governor: Sarojini Naidu (UP).
    • First Indian Nobel laureate: Rabindranath Tagore (Literature, 1913, Gitanjali). First Bharat Ratna recipients (1954): C. Rajagopalachari, C.V. Raman, S. Radhakrishnan.
    • First Olympic medal: Khashaba Jadhav (wrestling bronze, Helsinki 1952); first individual Olympic gold: Abhinav Bindra (shooting, Beijing 2008); first woman Olympic medal: Karnam Malleswari (weightlifting bronze, Sydney 2000).
    • First Indian in space: Rakesh Sharma (1984, Soviet Soyuz T-11; "Saare Jahan Se Achcha"). First Indian woman in space: Kalpana Chawla (1997; died in Columbia disaster, 2003).
    • First woman to climb Everest: Bachendri Pal (1984); first Indian woman IPS officer: Kiran Bedi; first woman IAS: Anna Rajam Malhotra; first woman judge of SC: Fathima Beevi.
    • First newspaper: Bengal Gazette (James Augustus Hicky, 1780). First census: 1872 (Lord Mayo); first regular decennial census: 1881 (Lord Ripon).

    National symbols & culture

    • National anthem: Jana Gana Mana (Rabindranath Tagore; adopted 24 Jan 1950; first sung 1911, Calcutta session). National song: Vande Mataram (Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, novel Anandamath).
    • National animal: Royal Bengal Tiger; bird: Indian Peacock; flower: Lotus; tree: Banyan; fruit: Mango; river: Ganga; aquatic animal: Ganges River Dolphin; heritage animal: Elephant.
    • Classical dances (state mapping — asked constantly): Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu; Kathak — Uttar Pradesh; Kathakali & Mohiniyattam — Kerala; Odissi — Odisha; Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh; Manipuri — Manipur; Sattriya — Assam.
    • Folk dances: Bihu (Assam), Bhangra (Punjab), Garba/Dandiya (Gujarat), Lavani (Maharashtra), Ghoomar (Rajasthan), Rouf (Kashmir), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Chhau (West Bengal/Jharkhand/Odisha).
    • Books & authors: Gitanjali — Tagore; Discovery of India / Glimpses of World History — Nehru; Hind Swaraj — Gandhi; Anandamath — Bankim Chandra; Godan — Premchand; Guide — R.K. Narayan; God of Small Things — Arundhati Roy; White Tiger — Aravind Adiga; Satanic Verses — Salman Rushdie; A Suitable Boy — Vikram Seth.
    • UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India: 40+ sites (approximate, growing). The most-asked: Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort, Khajuraho, Hampi, Konark Sun Temple, Mahabalipuram, Ellora & Ajanta Caves, Kaziranga & Manas (Assam), Sundarbans, Western Ghats, Dholavira (2021), Ramappa Temple (2021), Santiniketan (2023).

    Census 2011 (the fixed question bank)

    • Total population: 121.09 crore; decadal growth: 17.7%; sex ratio: 943 females per 1,000 males; literacy: 73% (male 80.9%, female 64.6%).
    • Most populous state: Uttar Pradesh; least: Sikkim. Highest density: Bihar; lowest: Arunachal Pradesh.
    • Highest literacy: Kerala (94%); lowest: Bihar (~61.8%). Highest sex ratio: Kerala (1,084); lowest: Haryana (879).
    • Most populous UT: Delhi; least populous UT: Lakshadweep. 2011 was the 15th Census of India.

    Sports quick-reference

    • Cricket: India has won the ODI World Cup twice — 1983 (Kapil Dev) and 2011 (M.S. Dhoni); T20 World Cups — 2007 and 2024 (Rohit Sharma). First World Cup: 1975 (West Indies won).
    • Hockey: India's national game in popular memory (not officially declared); India won 8 Olympic golds (1928–1980); Dhyan Chand — "the Wizard"; National Sports Day: 29 August (his birthday).
    • Awards: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna (highest — first: Viswanathan Anand); Arjuna Award; Dronacharya Award (coaches); Dadasaheb Phalke (cinema); Jnanpith (literature); Bharat Ratna (highest civilian).
    • Olympics: 2024 Paris (India: 1 silver, 5 bronze); upcoming Los Angeles 2028. FIFA World Cup 2026: USA–Canada–Mexico (June–July 2026). Winter Olympics 2026: Milano-Cortina, Italy (February 2026).

    Current Affairs 2025–26 (verified, figures approximate)

    • Bihar Assembly elections (Nov 2025): NDA won a landslide — 202 of 243 seats; Nitish Kumar sworn in as CM for a record 10th term; BJP became the single largest party (89 seats), JD(U) 85; RJD fell to 25, Congress to 6. Record 67.13% turnout, with women voters outnumbering men.
