    • ICC Champions Trophy 2025 (Feb–Mar): India won unbeaten, beating New Zealand in the final — Rohit Sharma's last ICC assignment as ODI captain.
    • ICC Women's ODI World Cup 2025 (hosted by India & Sri Lanka): India won its first-ever title, beating South Africa by 52 runs in the final; captain Harmanpreet Kaur; Player of the Match (final) Shafali Verma (87); Player of the Tournament Deepti Sharma.
    • Asia Cup 2025: India beat Pakistan in the final, completing a treble over Pakistan in the tournament. India also drew the Test series in England (2025) under new captain Shubman Gill after the retirements of Kohli and Rohit from Tests.
    • Chess: D. Gukesh became the youngest-ever World Chess Champion (December 2024, beating Ding Liren at 18) — expect this in 2025–26 papers.
    • G20: 2025 summit held in Johannesburg, South Africa (India had hosted in New Delhi, 2023 — theme "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam").
    • Space: ISRO's Gaganyaan crewed mission programme continued toward its first human spaceflight; Chandrayaan-3 (2023, first landing near the lunar south pole — lander Vikram, rover Pragyan) remains the anchor fact.
    • Economy: Union Budget presented 1 February each year by the Finance Minister; India's GDP growth remained among the fastest of major economies through 2024–25 (figures move quarterly — check the latest Economic Survey).
    • Schemes in the news: PM-KISAN instalments, Ayushman Bharat expansion to all senior citizens 70+ (announced 2024), Lakhpati Didi, PM Vishwakarma for artisans.
    • Days & themes: SSC loves "theme of the year" questions — World Environment Day (5 June), International Yoga Day (21 June, 11th edition in 2025), National Voters' Day (25 January). Themes change yearly; revise from the year's compilation.

    How to use this chapter: static GK is permanent — learn it cold. Current affairs expire: keep a rolling 12-month notebook, and in the final month before the exam, revise only the last 6 months. For any CA one-liner, the pattern is always who + what + where + when — that framing alone converts half the guesses into answers.

    15. Arithmetic Applications: Mixtures, Discount & Simplification

    SSC arithmetic rewards one skill above all: converting a wordy situation into a single ratio or a single multiplication. Mixtures, discount and simplification questions look different on the surface, but underneath they are all the same move — fix what does not change, and let everything else follow.

    15.1 Mixtures and alligation — the see-saw rule

    When two ingredients at prices p₁ and p₂ (p₁ < p₂) are mixed to a mean price m, the ratio of the cheaper to the dearer ingredient is (p₂ − m) : (m − p₁). Picture a see-saw: the mean sits closer to the ingredient used in larger quantity. Worked example: tea at Rs. 240 and Rs. 300 mixed to Rs. 270 gives (300 − 270) : (270 − 240) = 1:1. The same rule works on percentages, densities and profit rates — anywhere a weighted average appears. Repeated replacement: if a fraction f of a vessel is drawn and replaced n times, the original liquid left = initial × (1 − f)ⁿ. A 50-litre cask with 10 litres replaced twice keeps 50 × (4/5)² = 32 litres of wine. Milkman trick: selling a watered mixture at the cost price of pure milk, the gain percentage equals (water ÷ milk) × 100 — a 25% gain means water:milk = 1:4. Trap: in "how much must be added" questions, the quantity of the other ingredient is the constant — fix milk when water is added, fix water when milk (or spirit) is added.

    15.2 Discount — follow the price chain

    Every discount question is a chain: Cost → Marked → Selling. Mark-up then discount: marked 40% above cost with 15% off means 100 → 140 → 140 × 0.85 = 119, a 19% profit. Never add or subtract the percentages directly. Successive discounts: 20% then 25% leaves 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60 of the price, i.e. a 40% single equivalent — always less than the sum, because the second discount bites a smaller base. Three discounts of 10%, 20%, 30% leave 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.504, an effective 49.6%. Better-offer comparison: a single 30% discount beats two successive 15% discounts (which net only 27.75%) — when in doubt, multiply the "kept" fractions. Cash discount with profit: if cost is Rs. 800, profit 14% and cash discount 5%, first find selling price 800 × 1.14 = 912, then marked price = 912 ÷ 0.95 = Rs. 960. The order matters: profit is computed on cost, discount on the marked price. Exam shortcut: convert "discount d%" to the multiplier (1 − d/100) immediately and chain multiplications — it kills the common error of applying each discount to the original price.

    15.3 Simplification — speed without slips

    Simplification is won by recognising forms, not by grinding arithmetic. BODMAS discipline: in 72 ÷ 8 × 3 − 15 + 6 ÷ 2, do 9 × 3 = 27 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 first, then 27 − 15 + 3 = 15 — the trap is adding before multiplying. Identity radar: (1.2)² − (0.8)² collapses via a² − b² to 2.0 × 0.4 = 0.8; (0.75³ + 0.25³) ÷ (0.75² − 0.75×0.25 + 0.25²) collapses via a³ + b³ to 0.75 + 0.25 = 1.0; 999 × 999 + 2 × 999 + 1 is (999+1)² = 1,000,000. Train your eye to see these before touching the calculator in your head. Fraction equivalents: memorise 12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6, 14.28% = 1/7, 11.11% = 1/9, 33.33% = 1/3, 37.5% = 3/8 — "45% of 600 − 30% of 900 + 12.5% of 240" becomes 270 − 270 + 30 = 30 in seconds. Surds and roots: √3.24 = 1.8, √0.81 = 0.9, √1.21 = 1.1 — shift the decimal, root the number, shift back. ∛1331 = 11 and ∛3375 = 15 are worth memorising cold; they recur. Final habit: estimate before computing — if your exact answer for a discount chain is nowhere near the estimate, you applied a discount to the wrong base.

    16. Bihar Special GK: History, Geography & Culture

    Bihar is the heaviest-weighted state in SSC's static GK because it compresses two millennia of Indian history into one exam syllabus — Magadha's empires, the Buddha's enlightenment, the Mauryan capital, the Pala universities, Sher Shah's reforms and the freedom movement all happened here.

    16.1 Ancient Bihar — the imperial heartland

    Three of the sixteen Mahajanapadas — Magadha, Vajji (the Lichchhavi confederacy) and Anga — lay in present-day Bihar. Magadha rose under Bimbisara (founder of the Haryanka line, contemporary of the Buddha), expanded under Ajatashatru, passed to the Nandas under Mahapadma Nanda, and became the base of the Mauryan Empire when Chandragupta Maurya seized Pataliputra around 321 BCE. Ashoka ruled from Pataliputra and held the third Buddhist council there. The Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and Mahavira attained nirvana at Pawapuri; the first Buddhist council met at Rajgir (ancient Girivraja, Magadha's earliest capital). Nalanda University was founded by the Gupta king Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE; Vikramshila was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala in the 8th century and Odantapuri by Gopala. Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in the 7th century and left the most detailed foreign account of ancient Bihar.

    16.2 Medieval and modern milestones

    Sher Shah Suri, born in Sasaram where his grand tomb still stands, built the Grand Trunk Road and reformed revenue administration before the Mughals returned. The Battle of Buxar (1764), fought in Bihar, gave the British the Diwani of Bengal. In 1857, the octogenarian Kunwar Singh of Jagdispur led the revolt in Bihar. Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, fought for indigo farmers. Bihar's modern map was drawn in stages: carved from the Bengal Presidency as Bihar and Orissa province on 22 March 1912 (celebrated as Bihar Diwas), separated from Orissa in 1936, and bifurcated again in November 2000 when Jharkhand was created. Shri Krishna Sinha became the first Chief Minister in 1946; the Patna High Court dates to 1916.

    16.3 Geography and polity numbers to memorise

    Bihar has 38 districts in 9 divisions, with 40 Lok Sabha, 16 Rajya Sabha, 243 Assembly and 75 Legislative Council seats. The Ganga flows east across the state, joined by the Sone, Gandak, Bagmati and the Kosi — the Kosi's shifting course earned it the name "Sorrow of Bihar". Valmiki Tiger Reserve in West Champaran is the state's only tiger reserve. Official symbols: state bird the house sparrow, state tree the peepal, state flower the marigold, state fruit the mango, state song "Mere Bharat Ke Kanthahar", and the state animal the ox/bull per the state government's official list (the answer used in the 71st BPSC paper). The Golghar granary in Patna was built in 1786; the Barabar caves in Jehanabad are Mauryan-era rock-cut caves; the Sonpur fair in Saran district is among Asia's largest cattle fairs.

    16.4 Culture, language and economy

    Chhath is the state festival, dedicated to the Sun god; Sama Chakeva and Madhushravani are the other signature festivals. Folk dances include Jat-Jatin, Jhijhiya and Domkach. Hindi is the official language; Maithili entered the Eighth Schedule in 2003 (92nd Amendment), while Bhojpuri, Magahi and Angika dominate daily speech. GI-tagged pride includes Shahi Litchi of Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpuri silk, Mithila Makhana, Katarni rice, Sikki grass craft and Madhubani painting. Literary giants: Vidyapati (Maithil Kokil), Ramdhari Singh 'Dinkar' and Nagarjuna; freedom-era icons Dr. Rajendra Prasad (born at Ziradei, Siwan; India's first President), Jayaprakash Narayan (Sitab Diara, Saran) and Karpoori Thakur. Agriculture — rice, wheat, maize, pulses and litchi — still anchors the economy, which is why SSC frames so many Bihar questions around rivers, crops and fairs rather than industry.
